question: For the equation \(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}=\dfrac{N+1}{N}\) to be true where \(N\) is positive, \(x\) can have:
solution:
Solving for \(x\) will show how the condition \(N>0\) restricts its possible values. The original equation requires \(x\ne1\), and \(N>0\) already ensures \(N\ne0\). We may therefore multiply by \(N(1-x)\):
\[
N(1+x)=(N+1)(1-x).
\]
Expanding and collecting the terms containing \(x\) gives
\[
(2N+1)x=1,
\qquad x=\frac{1}{2N+1}.
\]
Since \(N>0\), the denominator is greater than \(1\), so \(0<x<1\).

We must also show that every value in this interval is possible. Given any \(0<x<1\), choose
\[
N=\frac{1-x}{2x}>0.
\]
Then both original denominators are nonzero, and
\[
\frac{N+1}{N}=\frac{1+x}{1-x}.
\]
Thus the possible values are exactly the positive numbers less than \(1\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
